# v0.8.5 - The Specification Rebuild and the Tier 2 Fix Pass

## What's Changed in v0.8.5

Two halves, and neither changes the protocol — which is why this is a patch release rather than the minor the documentation work was briefly planned as. The larger half is the documentation's *shape*, which had stopped doing its job. The smaller half closes the six items the v0.8.2 verification left in its Tier 2 list: a URL-parsing ambiguity, a snapshot-tool ordering defect that put excluded bytes into the object store, a repo-wide LFS setting that misroutes objects in a dual-remote setup, a release gate that tested one interpreter and checked its tag too late, a build with no install check, and three stale timings carried in CI.

`DESIGN.md` had become a changelog wearing a spec's clothes. Its second half was nine subsections titled `(v0.5.0)` through `(v0.8.0)`, each listing fixes under their review identifiers, with later entries silently superseding earlier ones — so a reader could not answer "what does the protocol guarantee *today*?" without replaying the release history, and the same material was already in the CHANGELOG in more detail. Worse, the parts that *were* normative had drifted: the storage diagram still tagged a directory with the release that introduced it, the sequence diagram showed a ref being uploaded to a path it is never uploaded to, and the credential section omitted the precedence rule that changed in v0.8.3.

### Changed

- **`DESIGN.md` rebuilt as a specification.** The document is now organised by what the system must do rather than by when it changed: **Invariants** (transport, storage, concurrency, data safety), **Protocol** (wire, on-server layout, API surface, lock, compaction, LFS, safety, configuration, modules), a **Failure Model** mapping every detectable failure to fail-closed, fail-loud or warn, a **Security & Threat Model**, and **Non-Goals**. Each old §7.x subsection was split into its invariant — which moved into the new structure — and its release narrative, which did not, because it is already in the CHANGELOG. Nothing normative was dropped: the split was checked identifier by identifier against the previous revision.
- **The stale parts are corrected.** The storage diagram no longer carries release tags; the sequence diagram now shows the settle window, the post-lock re-read, the final compare-and-swap read and the read-back, and shows the ref upload going to its parent directory; the credential section states the precedence rule; and the header no longer claims a status ("Ready for Upstream Integration") that nothing had established.

### Added

- **`SECURITY.md`** — credential handling and precedence, the token-scoping rule and why it exists, plain-HTTP and file-permission behaviour, TLS and proxy configuration, the threat model from an operator's angle, what the lock tickets disclose, and how to report a vulnerability.
- **`RUNBOOK.md`** — recovery procedures with symptom, cause and fix: a lock held by a machine that no longer exists, stray or conflicting refs, a ref pointing at a missing object, half-uploaded packfiles, conflict artifacts inside `refs/`, and a failed compaction after a successful push.
- **A supported-versions and compatibility matrix** (`DESIGN.md` §4.3.1). The documents claimed "all modern Seafile servers (CE and Pro)" while the suite validates against a stub; the matrix states what is claimed and marks what has not been exercised.
- **TLS and proxy guidance** (`USER_GUIDE` §6): `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` / `SSL_CERT_FILE`, `HTTPS_PROXY` / `NO_PROXY`, and the note that **Git's own `http.sslCAInfo` is not read** — the helper is a separate process, which is why a self-hosted instance can fail with a certificate error in a setup where a GitHub remote works.
- **Upgrade and compatibility notes** (`USER_GUIDE` §5): the v0.7.0 lock removal, the v0.8.4 grant marker's fleet-wide requirement, and the fact that no protocol marker file exists to make old and new clients refuse each other.
- **The dual-remote LFS trap is documented** (`USER_GUIDE` §11.1, pointed at from §8.5 and `DESIGN.md` §4.6). `lfs.standalonetransferagent` is *repo-wide*, so with it set to `seafile`, LFS objects route to Seafile even when the remote being pushed is GitHub — leaving pointers on GitHub with no objects behind them. The scoped `lfs.https://seafile.example.com/.standalonetransferagent` form, the second-setting trap in `lfs.customtransfer.seafile.args` (which names the destination a second time), and the `concurrent` default are all spelled out.

### Fixed

- **`USER_GUIDE` §6 documented the credential behaviour that v0.8.3 had already replaced.** It said a bare `SEAFILE_TOKEN` "is adopted for *any* server the remote URL names" — the confused-deputy defect A2 fixed, not the shipped behaviour. The code requires `SEAFILE_SERVER` alongside the token and ignores the token otherwise; the guide now says so, and a troubleshooting row names the error a user actually sees. A prose contradiction the doc guards cannot see, found by re-reading the section while writing `SECURITY.md`.

- **URL parsing (A7).** A dotted library name with a nested path was read as a server, so `seafile://notes.v2/team/repo` made `notes.v2` the host and `team` the library. The host test is now conservative: a port or userinfo is honoured outright, and a bare dot counts only when the segment has the shape of a real hostname — dot-separated labels ending in an *alphabetic* label — so `notes.v2` and `proj.2026` stay libraries. A name that is genuinely either way (`my.lib`, `files.local`) is still read as a server, and the explicit-scheme form names the server outright; the ambiguity is stated in `DESIGN.md` §4.3 and `USER_GUIDE` §7 rather than left to be discovered. Separately, `%2F` could smuggle a path separator past the `.`/`..` refusal, because segments were percent-decoded *after* being split; decoding now happens first. And `normalize_netloc()` read `urlparse(...).port` unguarded, so a malformed port escaped as urllib's bare `ValueError` — naming neither the URL nor the fact that the fault was a *URL* fault (A7.4). The shipped `contrib/seafile-client-context-menu.patch` generated a URL the helper misreads, a bare host with an unencoded library and folder, and now emits an explicit-scheme, percent-encoded URL.
- **An excluded path was read, hashed and written to the object store before being dropped (B2).** `build_snapshot` staged the whole tree with `git add -A -f .` and removed the excluded paths from the index afterwards — but the index is a *cache*, and a path that never reaches it cannot be skipped by it. Every excluded byte was read from disk, hashed, and written as a loose object, then left unreferenced. Excludes are now applied *before* staging (the post-filter stays as a safety net), so a large excluded tree costs nothing, and a test asserts that an excluded file produces no new object.
- **A local `gc` made the helper re-download packs it already had (A9).** The skip test compared the remote's pack *names* against the local pack directory, and a local `gc` repacks and renames them, so the comparison silently stopped matching. The installed set is now recorded per repository id and per destination in `.git/seafile/<repo-id>/packs.json`, written after each fetch, so the decision survives a repack; an unreadable or unknown-version state file costs a re-download, never a missing object.

### Tests & Tooling

- `tests/test_docs_consistency.py` gains `TestDesignIsASpecNotAChangelog`: the normative sections must be present, and no heading may name a release. The guards check *tokens* — config keys, environment variables, subcommands — not structure, so without this a future release could add `(v1.1)` headings back one at a time with every guard staying green.
- `tools/verify_docs_guards.py` gains two scenarios proving that guard catches drift: a renamed normative section, and a reintroduced release-stamped heading. 10 → 12 injected drifts.
- `SECURITY.md` and `RUNBOOK.md` joined the guarded document set and `MANIFEST.in`, so the existing guards now cover them and they reach the sdist. Both were written to satisfy those guards, which is how the dotted-name counter-example in an early draft of the runbook was caught before it shipped.
- **The release gate now tests the matrix it claims, and checks the tag first.** It ran a single `ubuntu-latest` / 3.11 combination, and the tag-versus-`__version__` assertion ran *after* the suite, so a mis-tagged release did all the work before failing. A `verify-tag` job now runs first, the `test` job `needs` it, and the gate carries the same `os` / `python-version` matrix with `fail-fast: false` as `ci.yml`.
- **The build now installs what it built.** `python -m build` was followed by an upload with no `twine check`, no wheel install, and nothing asserting that `tools/` stayed out of the wheel. `.github/smoke_install_wheel.sh` checks both artifacts with `twine check`, installs the wheel into a fresh venv, runs `git-remote-seafile version`, asserts the wheel has no top-level `tools/`, and asserts the sdist *does* ship `tools/seafile_snapshot.py`.
- **The stale timing curve in `ci.yml` is gone, and the doc guards run in CI.** `ci.yml` still quoted a curve measured at 268 tests, and `tools/verify_docs_guards.py` — which proves each guard catches drift — had no caller under `.github/` or `tests/`, so the proof never ran. The lint job now runs the guard tests and the drift scenarios, and the curve is a pointer to `CONTRIBUTING.md`.
- Suite: 640 → 671 tests / 123 → 130 targets, all green; docs guards 12/12; ruff clean.
